canberra.title: ACT Scouts’ spiritual home to rise from the ashes of ’03 bushfires
canberra.snippet: Since 2003, Scouts ACT has been without a permanent shelter at its spiritual home at Camp Cottermouth after deadly bushfires tore through...
canberra.content:
17 October 2026

Start the conversation

The Lions Club of Canberra Valley presented Scouts ACT with a cheque for $35,700 to build a new permanent building at Camp Cottermouth. Photo: Lions Club of Canberra Valley.

Since 2003, Scouts ACT has been without a permanent shelter at its spiritual home at Camp Cottermouth after deadly bushfires tore through the site, leaving the former training hall as nothing but ash.

More than two decades later the popular campsite is set to rise again, with longtime Scouts ACT partners, The Lions Club, raising more than $35,000 to build a new permanent shelter at the site.

Scouts ACT first began using Camp Cottermouth as a teaching site for Scouts back in the early 1950s.

However, after the bushfires, the lack of facilities limited the activities and opportunities that young people could take part in.

Now, with the money raised by the Lions Club, Scouts ACT Honorary Commissioner Neville Tomkins is confident the site can return to its former glory.

Mr Tomkins said Scouts and Lions shared identical values, which had made the organisations’ partnership very fruitful.

“We are both organisations dedicated to community service and helping others in our communities,” he said.

“The Scouts have been doing that for 118 years in Australia, while Lions Club are coming up on 80 years.

“We both believe that having a camp shelter at Camp Cottermouth is absolutely vital to the safety of our young people, as well as their experiences outdoors here in the ACT.

“For that, we can’t thank Lions Club enough.”

President of the Lions Club of Canberra Valley David Tate echoed those sentiments, saying the new facility would serve as more than just a training venue for the Scouts; it would also serve the wider Stromlo community.

“The contribution has reinvigorated a longstanding partnership between Lions and Scouts ACT, reflecting their shared commitment to youth development and community service,” he said.

“We are delighted to support Scouts ACT to extend the world-renowned youth program to more children in our local communities, through the donation of $35,700 to help build a camp shelter at Camp Cottermouth.”

The new indoor facility is expected to begin construction in 2027.

canberra.title: Can lived experience help break Canberra’s cycle of psychiatric readmissions?
canberra.snippet: When Keith Mahar was first diagnosed with bipolar disorder, he struggled with shame, stigma, and the belief that his life might never ret...
canberra.content:
Mental Health Minister Marisa Paterson joins Canberra Health Services staff and peer workers at the launch of Peer Pathways, a new program supporting patients through mental health treatment and recovery. Photo: Naziya Alvi.

When Keith Mahar was first diagnosed with bipolar disorder, he struggled with shame, stigma, and the belief that his life might never return to normal.

Twenty-five years after moving to Canberra, he is drawing on that experience to help others facing some of their darkest moments.

Mr Mahar is one of four peer workers employed under Peer Pathways, a new Canberra Health Services program that places people with lived experience of mental illness alongside patients receiving inpatient psychiatric care.

The program offers something clinical treatment alone cannot always provide: a conversation with someone who has been through a similar experience.

Mr Mahar recalled meeting a patient who sat slumped in a chair, avoiding eye contact, as clinicians introduced themselves. When he mentioned his own experience of bipolar disorder, the patient’s response was immediate.

“It was like he was hit by electricity and his head snapped up and he made contact with me,” Mr Mahar said.

“He was no longer the only person in that room with a lived experience of mental illness.”

The program has begun in Ward 12B at Canberra Hospital and the Acacia unit at North Canberra Hospital, both low-dependency adult mental health units.

Peer workers provide emotional and practical support, help patients understand their rights and treatment options, and assist with discharge planning. With patient consent, they can also support families and carers.

But while the initiative has been welcomed as a step towards more compassionate mental health care, its limited rollout raises questions about how many patients will benefit and whether it can help address broader pressures on Canberra’s mental health system.

The latest Canberra Health Services annual report shows 18 per cent of acute psychiatric patients were readmitted within 28 days, above the target of 17 per cent.

Mental Health Minister Marisa Paterson acknowledged the need to improve support for patients returning to the community.

However the eight-week community support component remains part of the intended expansion, rather than the fully established first stage.

Canberra Health Services director of lived experience Genevieve Whitlam said the model was informed by a NSW peer-supported transfer-of-care program, which had shown improvements in recovery outcomes and engagement with community services, alongside fewer early readmissions.

She said the approach recognised that recovery involved more than medication and clinical appointments.

Ms Whitlam spoke openly about her own experience of postnatal psychosis, describing the fear and loss of identity that followed her diagnosis.

“I was suddenly defined by my illness,” she said. “I was scared about recovery and I did not know what my future would hold.”

Connecting with other women who had experienced the same illness helped her regain confidence and imagine a future beyond hospital.

That understanding now sits at the centre of Peer Pathways.

“Through purposeful sharing of their lived experience, our peer workers can create conversations grounded in connection, understanding and hope,” she said.

Yet questions remain about the program’s reach. An independent inquiry into Dhulwa Secure Mental Health Unit previously recommended stronger lived-experience representation in multidisciplinary teams.

Asked whether peer workers would eventually be introduced at Dhulwa, Dr Paterson said expansion was possible but stopped short of providing a commitment or timeframe.

“Potentially, so what we’re doing here is really strengthening, developing the model … and then the idea is that, hopefully we can roll it out and expand the service across more parts of the mental health service,” she said.

Staff safety is another challenge. Canberra Health Services has previously faced scrutiny over occupational violence and its management of workplace psychological risks.

Asked how peer workers would be protected, Dr Paterson said significant work had been undertaken to improve violence prevention, de-escalation, incident investigations and support for affected staff. She said occupational violence remained a priority for reform.

canberra.title: Side Chick knows the way to a potato-lover’s heart
canberra.snippet: In a week when I needed comfort and, quite frankly, dinner delivered to my door, I turned to Side Chick. I have a soft spot for anything ...
canberra.content:
Side Chick delivers bagfuls of satisfyingly salty fare. Photos: Sophia Brady.

In a week when I needed comfort and, quite frankly, dinner delivered to my door, I turned to Side Chick.

I have a soft spot for anything Alex and Nicole Piris touch. One of the most memorable meals I have had in Canberra was at one of Fox and Bow’s Spanish dinner nights. The café transformed under low lights and candlelight, while the food was deeply personal and rooted in family tradition.

At a time when I was grieving the loss of my grandfather and emerging from the emotional fog of COVID, there was something incredibly comforting about being fed ancestral recipes prepared with such care.

Before that, in 2018, I wrote about the opening of their other venture, Manolo’s, in Phillip, where a bowl of seafood chowder remains firmly lodged in my mind.

So when Side Chick opened, I was curious. What would the family behind Fox and Bow do with one of Australia’s great institutions – the old-school takeaway shop?

While I was keen to check out the colourful new fit-out in person, circumstances meant I ordered from home instead. This quickly became what can only be described as a highly committed potato tasting.

The food menu centres on charcoal chicken, burgers, rolls, and salads, but the potatoes caught my attention. As a committed potato enthusiast, ordering four different varieties felt good.

As a committed potato enthusiast, I appreciated the skin on Chicken Fat Potatoes.

First up were the Chicken Fat Potatoes. They had the skin-on, which I appreciate. Roasted beneath the chickens as they cook, they soak up all those glorious drippings. Crisp around the edges and fluffy in the middle.

Next came the thick-cut chips. Rustic, gnarly, and gloriously non-uniform, they looked hand-cut rather than machine-produced. At first glance, they looked almost too crisp, but they struck that elusive balance between a crunchy exterior and a nice centre. The seasoning was top-notch.

Then there were the hashies and potato scallops, which raise an important question. What is the difference, and do you need both? The answer is yes, you do need both.

The hashies, made from grated potato, were golden, crisp and soft all at once. The potato scallops delivered all the deep-fried goodness you could hope for, with crisp batter wrapped around tender potato. Importantly, they were both a sensible size, not giant monsters.

Side Chick’s potato game is strong. These tasted like real potatoes, not frozen packets of stuff. And the seasoning? Excellent. Whoever is working the potato seasoning station, my tastebuds thank you.

One thing I could not scoff down quickly enough was the Chicken Gravy Roll. The long bread roll had been lightly toasted and buttered on the inside, a surprisingly considerate and time-intensive choice for takeaway food. Generous lashings of charcoal chicken were tucked inside, then absolutely drenched in gravy. As I ate, the bread slowly soaked it all up.

It was gloriously messy, an excellent sandwich!

The Chicken Schnitty Burger was equally generous. The schnitzel extended well beyond the edges of the bun and both sides were slathered in a tangy pickle-based sauce. The schnitzel itself was crisp, golden and tasted like actual chicken.

The Chicken Schnitty Burger was equally generous. The schnitzel extended well beyond the edges of the bun.

I was not sure why I ordered the chicken tenders. Aren’t tenders meant to be for children? Regardless, I was very happy with my life choices. Thick, chaotically shaped, heavily battered, and deeply golden, they were immensely satisfying. The only thing missing was a dipping sauce. More gravy would have been nice.

As for the charcoal chicken itself, it arrived plump and juicy, with juices running the moment I opened the bag. It was tender and well-cooked but perhaps the least interesting thing we ate.

The chicken and gravy roll was a gloriously messy, excellent sandwich!

Side Chick understands something important about takeaway food. Sometimes the day calls for a bag of salty potatoes done well. There is a wonderful episode of the Irish sitcom show Derry Girls where the family is devastated after being banned from their local chippy. Having just eaten my way through four different potato products, I can’t say they were overreacting.

Side Chick is located at 10 Chaseling Street, Phillip. They are open Wednesday to Sunday from 10 am to 7:30 pm.

canberra.title: Accused child abuse offender allegedly had inappropriate contact with girl in Ukraine
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse. Border force officials stopped a Canberra defence worker when he arrived bac...
canberra.content:
Nicholas Tyson Quinn, 42, had arrived back at Sydney International Airport when he was stopped by Australian Border Force officials. Photo: Sydney Airport Facebook.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged child abuse.

Border force officials stopped a Canberra defence worker when he arrived back in Australia before allegedly discovering he possessed child abuse material on his electronic devices.

In addition, the ACT Magistrates Court heard it was alleged 42-year-old Nicholas Tyson Quinn of Chisholm had been having inappropriate contact with a young girl in Ukraine for some time.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said Mr Quinn had flown into Sydney International Airport in May 2026 when Australian Border Force (ABF) officials selected him for an examination.

After looking at his electronic devices, the officers allegedly found child exploitation imagery and inappropriate conversations on a messaging application.

There were also suggestions that he had allegedly sent multiple sums of money to a teenager in Europe.

“The matter was referred to ACT Policing and enquiries relating to the man were conducted,” the police spokesperson said.

Police raided the home where Mr Quinn lived with his mother earlier this week, allegedly finding more child exploitation material on a USB that was plugged into his computer.

Mr Quinn, who has worked in the payroll department of an Australian Defence Force contractor for the past four years, was charged with two counts of possessing child abuse material before he faced the Magistrates Court on Friday 16 October.

The court heard it was also alleged he had been having inappropriate contact with a woman and her young daughter in the Ukraine.

While the daughter was now 17, it was alleged he may have known the pair for the past eight years. ABF records showed he visited Ukraine in 2018.

The prosecutor from the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions said police had not yet identified the people in the 130 photos and videos of alleged child abuse material. This meant they did not know if the material depicted the girl from Ukraine.

But the court heard the implication from an alleged conversation between the pair suggested that Mr Quinn had seen the girl’s genitals.

The prosecutor also alleged the USB that police seized from his home, which allegedly contained child abuse material, had been accessed earlier this week. This meant he was alleged to have accessed the material recently, even though he knew the ABF had examined his devices at the airport earlier this year.

When opposing bail, the prosecutor said she was concerned about Mr Quinn’s flight risk. As a dual citizen of Australia and Latvia, he could go to the Latvian embassy to obtain a new passport even if he surrendered his current one.

Mr Quinn’s lawyer, Duncan Errey of Legal Aid, accepted the allegations against his client were serious.

“These matters are destined for the Supreme Court one way or another,” he said, noting a trial might not be able to take place until 2028 if his client pleaded not guilty.

Mr Errey said his client had a complicated medical history, including Type 1 diabetes, so would “feel the burden” of being remanded in custody if bail was refused.

Magistrate Alexandra Burt accepted there was currently a high degree of speculation in the prosecution’s case against Mr Quinn, as the extent of his alleged connection to the girl wasn’t yet known.

She also said the prosecutor couldn’t answer some questions about the case that went to the risks of granting him bail.

However, Magistrate Burt ultimately thought the risks of releasing him did justify his detention and refused his bail application.

Mr Quinn, who requires a security clearance to work at the defence force contractor, was remanded in custody and the matter was adjourned to 5 November. No pleas were entered.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call Triple Zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

canberra.title: A century of bowls, friendships and survival: Canberra Bowling Club turns 100
canberra.snippet: When a small group of enthusiasts gathered beside Hotel Canberra on Christmas Eve in 1925, they were making history without knowing it. T...
canberra.content:
Canberra Bowling Club, Forrest, is celebrating its history. Photo: James Coleman.

When a small group of enthusiasts gathered beside Hotel Canberra on Christmas Eve in 1925, they were making history without knowing it.

They were the first people to play lawn bowls in the fledgling national capital, on a green established by the Federal Capital Commission.

A century later, Canberra Bowling Club is still going strong, having survived changing times, financial pressures and the closure of other community clubs.

As the club prepares to celebrate its centenary, secretary Stephen Murphy believes its history is closely connected to the story of Canberra itself.

“We believe that as the club has been a part of the Canberra community for this length of time, the history would be of interest to some of your readers,” he said.

For its long-time members, however, the club’s greatest achievement is not simply reaching 100 years. It remains a place where people can meet, play sports and feel part of a community.

Life member and former president Geoff McKay, who has been associated with the club for about a decade, believes its independence has been central to its survival.

“It’s one of the few surviving clubs in Canberra, and it is actually owned by the members,” he said.

As other clubs closed or were absorbed into larger organisations, some of their members found a new home at Canberra Bowling Club.

Mr McKay credits successive committees with managing the club responsibly and maintaining its welcoming atmosphere.

“It’s a wonderful place to meet people and I play bowls quite regularly,” he said.

He believes the social connection is particularly valuable for older Canberrans.

“I feel that sport’s terribly important, particularly among the older generation, to keep them active and congregating and socializing.”

The club’s history stretches back to Canberra’s earliest years.

Following that first game in December 1925, local bowlers met at Hotel Canberra on 24 September 1926 to establish a club. The Canberra Bowling Club name was formally adopted on 27 October, with 27 foundation members.

Its first season began the following month and, by December, members were playing their first inter-club match against Goulburn.

As the capital grew, so did the club. It moved to its permanent home in Forrest, where a new green and weatherboard clubhouse were completed in 1931. Governor-General Sir Isaac Isaacs officially opened the green later that year.

Over the following decades, it became a gathering place for public servants, diplomats and local families. Additional greens opened in 1936 and 1948, while the Canberra Forrest Women’s Bowling Club was established in 1978 with 13 foundation members.

The clubhouse was rebuilt in the 1990s after the ageing structure suffered extensive damage from borers and white ants, with the new building opening in April 1995.

But keeping a century-old sporting club financially viable has required more than preserving its history.

Former president and life member Dave Kimber joined in 2008 after moving into apartments next door. He went on to serve three separate terms as president, totalling nine years.

At the time, he said, the club was struggling financially.

One of the most important decisions was replacing its two grass greens with synthetic surfaces in 2015–16, making it the first all-synthetic bowling club in the ACT.

Mr Kimber believes the change helped secure the club’s future by reducing maintenance costs and allowing the greens to be used more consistently.

“Basically if we hadn’t, you know, taken that direction, we would have gone broke by now,” he said.

The next challenge was attracting people beyond the traditional bowling community.

In 2025, the club voluntarily surrendered its poker machine licences, becoming a pokie-free venue. Funds from the ACT Government’s surrender scheme are now being directed towards outdoor hospitality areas and live-music facilities.

Mr Kimber, who was involved in the decision, said removing the machines also made the club more appealing for weddings, birthdays and other celebrations.

Today, Sunday afternoon live music brings another crowd through the doors, while barefoot bowls introduce newcomers to the sport.

“If you’ve got 70 or 80 people in our club listening to music, it’s actually quite a buzz,” Mr Kimber said.

He still visits about three times a week and sees the club as an important social outlet for retired Canberrans.

“It’s important that they get that opportunity to socialize during the week and indeed it’s good exercise for them.”

Mr McKay, who served as president for about eight years across separate terms, said the club’s modest size was part of its charm. With roughly 120 bowling and social members, it remains a place where people can get to know one another.

To mark its centenary, Canberra Bowling Club will hold an open day on Saturday 31 October, from 10 am to 8 pm, inviting the community to celebrate a century of sport and social life in the capital. Further details are available here.

australia.title: Mexican judge sentences three men to 158 years in prison for murders of Australian and US surfers​
australia.snippet: Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend Carter Rhoad, were killed while on a surf trip in Baja Califo...
australia.content:
A Mexican ⁠judge ⁠has sentenced ​three men to 158 years ⁠and nine months in prison each for ⁠the murder of ​two Australian ‌brothers ‌and their American friend during ‌a 2024 surf trip to the state of Baja California.

The ‌defendants were declared guilty a week ​ago of homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft ⁠with violence, crimes committed against ​Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend ​Carter Rhoad.

Rhoad and the Robinsons were shot dead in a suspected robbery while travelling through Mexico.

They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on 27 April 2024.

Their bodies were found days later in a clifftop well with gunshot wounds to the heads.

Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons.

Two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were also found guilty and have been sentenced.

The families of the victims followed the sentencing hearing via video link.

Prosecutors had requested damages of more than $100,000 but the judge ruled against it and said any compensation would have to be pursued through civil proceedings.

The brothers’ parents, Martin and Debra Robinson, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.

They have established a foundation in their sons’ names to carry on their legacy.

The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”.

Callum, the older of the two brothers, moved to the US as a professional lacrosse player and has been remembered for his loving nature and passion for the environment, having been involved in coastal cleanups.

Jake, a doctor, was set to take up a position at Geelong hospital after returning to Australia.

He has been remembered for his academic success, his passion for sport, particularly cricket and surfing, and his compassion.

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.

Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

australia.title: Mimicking populists will not ease cost of living or boost productivity, Mathias Cormann warns
australia.snippet: Former minister and OECD head urges Australia not to adopt migration caps, with research showing migrants boost employment Get our breaki...
australia.content:
Australia’s mainstream political parties are being warned not to adopt populist policies such as migration caps to address voters’ grievances over the cost of living.

Instead, Australia’s longest-serving finance minister, Mathias Cormann, is urging politicians to deliver housing, real wage growth and lower energy costs by boosting productivity.

Now the secretary general for the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Cormann will deliver an address to the Centre for Independent Studies on Saturday night spruiking productivity as the only way to reliably lower the cost of living over the long term.

Though not directly named in his address, One Nation – which largely runs on an anti-immigration platform – has surged in popularity since the 2025 federal election, with its primary vote reaching 25%, according to the latest Guardian Essential poll, rising above the Coalition’s 22%.

While populist parties may have gained traction by speaking to real grievances about rising energy bills, home ownership and real incomes going backwards, Cormann is expected to warn Labor and the Coalition not to follow suit.

“Mainstream parties that respond to a populist surge by adopting its economics do not recover their voters. They lose twice: once to the original, which the electorate will always prefer to the copy, and once to the centre, which has nowhere else to go,” he will say in his address.

“The lesson is consistent: deliver homes, lower energy costs, real wage growth and a credible budget, and the populist tide recedes.

“Mimic the populists, and you simply confirm that they were right all along. The way to defeat populism is to solve the problems it feeds on.”

Cormann will point to “arbitrary migration caps” imposed regardless of their effect on business, hospitals, aged care or universities.

He will acknowledge more Australians now than any time in the past 20 years say the migration intake is too high and may support such policies, with many attributing their concerns to housing.

But the answer is to address housing supply, infrastructure, services and the composition of the migration intake, he will say.

According to OECD research across Australia’s regions, in places where more migrants arrived, employment among Australian-born workers grew faster, not slower, with no measurable effect on their wages.

Without migration, Australia’s working-age population would decrease as the number of older people grows.

“An ageing country that chooses to shrink its working-age population while promising to spend more on health, care and defence has not developed a plan – it has put forward a contradiction,” Cormann will say.

Tariffs, which have been imposed by US president Donald Trump and proposed by One Nation, would also fail to address the cost of living and could instead raise costs for farmers, miners and builders, Cormann will say.

He believes Australia can only grow its way out of the issue through productivity.

“There is no shortcut to a lower cost of living. There is no populist shortcut, through tariffs and caps and state banks,” he will say.

“There is only the long way round: an economy that produces more, competes harder and grows faster than its costs … anyone offering you a quicker route is offering you a poorer country.”

australia.title: Gone to the dogs: racing fans mourn closure of ‘Wenty’, Sydney’s historic greyhound track
australia.snippet: Thousands pack Wentworth Park for the final time before the stadium is demolished and returned to parkland Get our breaking news email , ...
australia.content:
The end of an era has fallen upon an Australian sporting landmark as the greyhound races at an inner-city track kicked off for the very last time.

Thousands packed into Wentworth Park in central Sydney on Friday night, where greyhound races have been held since 1932, for the last race meeting before the track’s planned demolition.

The final race of the night was the richest in the world – the Million Dollar Chase – and was won by Magical Ang.

For Geoff Rose, the closure was a sign of the times – the land in the inner-west suburb of Glebe is worth a fortune in a city where growth will not slow down.

But the NSW Greyhound Breeders, Owners and Trainers Association chair remained sad to see the park go.

“It is quite heartbreaking to a lot of people,” he said.

Another spectator mourning the closure was Jeff Collerson, a veteran greyhound writer who first set foot on the track at Wentworth Park in December 1962 as a 17-year-old cadet journalist.

Now 81, he was trackside as the dogs raced around the circuit, nestled against the Sydney city skyline, for the final time and reminisced about his career.

He said the closure of what locals refer to affectionately as “Wenty” was tragic.

“I remember saying to my wife years ago, I want you to cast my ashes in front of the winning post at Wentworth Park, but I told her not to do that now,” Collerson said.

“Wentworth Park’s got a special aura about it that the other tracks won’t have … it’s got a special buzz to it.

“That will be lost forever because having a city track is just fantastic.”

All buildings are slated for demolition after October 2027, and the site is planned to be returned to parkland under the auspices of Sydney’s council.

Wentworth Park was created between 1876 and 1880 using silt dredged from Sydney’s harbour. Greyhound racing began in the park in 1932, and by the 1970s, the sport was attracting large crowds.

Greyhound Racing NSW, the state’s regulator for the sport, announced this week it had chosen the existing Richmond race club, about an hour north-west of central Sydney, as the replacement site for the industry.

Rose said his association was also exploring another option, which could see it establishing race meetings at a site near Appin, south-west of Sydney.

Either way, the state’s racing minister, David Harris, has previously promised $10m in government funding to help the industry find a new home – a move criticised by those calling for the industry to be shut down altogether.

Some have welcomed the track’s closure as a move towards the whole industry’s end.

A crowd of protesters stood outside the park as punters filed in, chanting that the sport kills dogs, and calling for an end to taxpayer dollars propping up the industry.

Aleisha Kernan and Kirsten Lambros work for Greyhounds as Pets, which helps facilitate the adoption of retired racing dogs.

Kernan said the sport’s potential new facilities would “open new avenues”.

“I think people should look at the future as well,” she said.

But for one young punter, Harry Dunlop, nothing would replace what he described as a “prominent piece of Australia”.

“It’s very unlikely that we’ll be going out to Richmond,” he said.

australia.title: Mortgage repayments are now cheaper than rent in some Australian suburbs. Is yours among them?
australia.snippet: As house prices plateau, the gap between the cost of buying and renting is narrowing in dozens of suburbs Get our breaking news email , f...
australia.content:
High rents and falling property prices have opened a rare window for Australian tenants to become homeowners, with mortgage repayments cheaper than rent in dozens of suburbs.

Guardian Australia’s analysis of Cotality data shows that median rents in inner-city Melbourne, suburban Canberra and Darwin are now nearly matching weekly home loan repayments.

In one in 10 suburbs and towns across the country, repayments are less than $200 a week higher than rent, for the typical property. In some suburbs, they are actually cheaper.

Australia’s median rent prices rose 5.5% over the year to September to reach $713 per week, Cotality data shows. The median property price across houses and units was flat over the year, after six months of steady falls.

The typical rent for a Melbourne apartment was $628 a week after rising 4.8% over the last year.

The typical repayments for a Melbourne flat were $211 more, or $839 a week, based on a median value of $624,740 in September, down nearly $25,000 from a year earlier.

The analysis assumes a new 30-year loan of 95% of the value, at a 6.2% interest rate. It does not account for any additional costs. Smaller loans made with bigger deposits would make repayments even more affordable compared with rents.

Owner-occupiers purchasing with a 5% deposit would typically do so through the government’s low deposit scheme, which is designed to help first home buyers.

Repayments were cheaper than rent for the typical property in Carlton, Melbourne CBD, Notting Hill, Travancore and Southbank.

Repayments on new loans had risen overall in the last year for most suburbs, as lower values were offset by interest rates rising 1 percentage point. Where values had fallen more than 10%, though, repayments were likely lower.

Clint Waters, a Melbourne mortgage broker, said home buying interest had dropped but renters were inquiring in strong numbers as they weighed lower house prices against higher rents.

“They’re certainly doing the maths … [and] the equation at the moment is starting to narrow,” Waters said.

Waters, director at Axton Finance, said a stable or growing number were looking to buy direct from their landlord, making the switch without moving.

“Landlords are getting slammed left, right and centre, and going ‘screw this, I’m going to offload,’” Waters said. “Tenants will ring us up and say, ‘I need to work out if I’ve got the capacity to buy this thing.’”

New apartments pushing down prices

In Sydney, repayments were just $100 a week more than rents in inner-city Ultimo and western suburbs Warwick Farm, Rosehill, Liverpool and Granville.

In the Canberra suburbs of Belconnen and Phillip, repayments were less than $75 a week more than rents. If only apartments are included, Braddon, Lyons, Gungahlin and Harrison join the list.

Gerard Burg, a Cotality researcher, said areas with significant apartment development tended to be cheaper to buy than rent, especially where flats were being sold direct to owner-occupiers and not rented out.

“That just [shows] this influx of supply pushing down the value of the purchase, while comparatively tight rental availability had led to this increase in rents,” Burg said.

But such areas were “anomalies”, he said. Houses remain generally more expensive to buy than rent.

“If it was a sustained thing that you could buy a property more cheaply than renting it, then everyone would buy and everyone would exit the rental market,” Burg said.

It was cheaper to buy in a quarter of suburbs in Darwin, where rents have risen 11.6% in the year. Most areas where buying was cheaper than renting were mining or resource project areas in which fly-in fly-out workers temporarily rent rather than buy, Burg said.

Burg said mortgage repayments would likely fall if the Reserve Bank held rates steady and values kept falling, as expected by financial markets, potentially narrowing the gap with rents.

“[With] rents continuing to increase or … go sideways, that could occur.”

australia.title: Cloudy with a chance of moths: bogong swarms are bamboozling weather radars across NSW
australia.snippet: Radar systems designed for rain, hail and snow are picking up bogong moths migrating to the Australian Alps Get our breaking news email ,...
australia.content:
It was during Sydney’s Olympic Games in 2000, people say, that a swarm of bogong moths attracted by stadium lights was so huge that meteorologists mistook it for rain.

Fast forward 26 years and the bogongs are back in big numbers. And, this time, they are firmly on the radar.

“Every single night, particularly across eastern New South Wales and around Sydney, widespread rain is appearing on the imagery,” the ABC’s meteorologist has reported.

“The only problem is, many nights (it’s appearing where) there hasn’t been a drop of rain (on the ground).”

Weather radars, designed for rain, hail or snow, may be picking up swarms of moths on their long-distance migration to the Australian Alps. Radio pulses, designed to hit water particles and bounce back as “echoes” on the rain radar screen, may be reflecting off insect bodies and wings instead.

A Bureau of Meteorology spokesperson says it is possible radars across eastern NSW are detecting bogong moths, as large numbers of insects can look like very light widespread rain, particularly near sunrise and sunset.

Radars have been showing increased echoes that aren’t rain, the spokesperson says, however completely attributing the effect to moths was challenging, given other factors, such as temperature inversions, can cause similar effects.

That radar data could be “absolute gold” for scientists, says Dr Kate Umbers, who has been working to understand where bogong moths breed and the routes they take.

After all, researchers have tried numerous tactics – from tagging tiny moths, to collecting stories and newspaper reports – to trace the moths’ journey across hundreds of kilometres.

Umbers, an associate professor in zoology at Western Sydney University and the managing director of Invertebrates Australia, says it poses all sorts of interesting possibilities and questions, including: “How many bogong moths equals heavy rain?”

But moths are far from the only flying animal able to be picked up by radar.

Prof Justin Welbergen, an ecologist who specialises in flying foxes at Western Sydney University, has been using radar data to track the movements of flying foxes, both in near real time and retrospectively.

It began, Welbergen says, because he had been researching the coordinated nightly departure of bats from their roosts, and happened to check the weather radar while in Melbourne.

“I decided to look at the weather radar to see if I could see any signal of the flying foxes in the radar – and there it was. And the rest was history.”

Flying fox emergences are highly organised events, where the hungriest individuals leave first, he says. “Adult females were followed by their young, and then the adult males would be the last ones to leave, only after all the females had left.”

The animals show up clearly in radar data as “a big bag of water”, emerging at about the same time each night around dusk, and flying in predictable directions, Welbergen says.

With those insights, researchers built a working prototype that allows them to track and count flying foxes using radar data – in near real time with the help of a computer algorithm, and even reconstruct historical movements over several decades with data from weather stations.

A similar initiative in the United States, called BirdCast, relies on weather radar to track bird migrations.

Welbergen hopes to expand the flying fox prototype, known as “Aerocast”, in collaboration with other researchers and organisations, for tracking other aerial animals, such as birds and even bogong moths. Although dependent on radar coverage and quality, it is a promising tool for conservation, which could be used to detect signals of important ecological events, such as mass flowering or extreme heat.

Like bogong moths, flying foxes are difficult to track across the landscape because of their extreme mobility. “Flying foxes travel all over the place, all the time. They congregate in these roosts, and the individuals that are there may not be there the next day.”

It is not the only thing the two species have in common, Welbergen says. “They often emerge from these central locations at predictable places, and predictable times of the day and year,” he says. “So our techniques for detecting flying foxes, I expect, are readily transferable to moths as well, because [on the radar] flying foxes are effectively just giant moths.”

In the meantime, Umbers has been delighted to have the help of millions of research assistants across Sydney and Canberra as the latest bogong wave passes through. “For us, having that many eyes on this species at one time is the best possible scenario we could hope for in trying to understand them.”

It has been a worrying few years since populations collapsed, but the small, brown critters are not out of the woods just yet. Their alpine habitat remains threatened by global heating, and an abundance of sightings in cities may not necessarily equate to a population boom overall.

Still, Umbers says it is “wonderful” that a new cohort of Australians are getting acquainted with a bogong moth storm. “There’s a lot of people alive that have never seen this,” she says. “The moths are saying: don’t forget about us, look after us, look how amazing and impactful and epic we can be.”

world.title: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested
world.snippet: At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports Mass arrests, forced ...
world.content:
Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.

More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.

The intensifying crackdown comes as the law criminalising homosexuality in the country was toughened earlier this year. On 11 March, Senegal’s parliament amended the penal code, doubling the maximum prison term for consensual same-sex relations to 10 years.

The new law introduced penalties of up to seven years in prison and a fine of 500,000 to 5m CFA francs (£650–£6,500) for promoting homosexuality, or supporting or financing LGBTQ+ people and organisations.

Larissa Kojoué, LGBTQ+ rights researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “LGBTQ+ people are being forced to curb their normal activities … for fear of arrest and increased stigma. Senegal’s government should call a halt to this crackdown, which threatens everyone’s rights.”

Same-sex sexual activity was criminalised in Senegal in 1965, but hostility towards LGBTQ+ individuals has grown in recent years. During the 2024 presidential campaign, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, who ended up winning the election, and the former prime minister Ousmane Sonko promised to strengthen laws criminalising same-sex relations, framing the issue as a national priority.

Arrests of men and women have happened all over the country. The police say they have arrested people based on information extracted from seized phones, third-party allegations or raids on private premises.

The changes to the penal code have had a chilling effect on lawyers, who said they were afraid to represent people for fear of being prosecuted themselves, according to the report. Doctors told Human Rights Watch that the changes were discouraging people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.

While there was a 49% fall in new HIV infections in western and central Africa from 2010 to 2022, sub-Saharan Africa remains disproportionately affected by the virus, with 64% of all people living with HIV globally.

Sylvie Beaumont, a consultant with HIV Justice Network, said she had received anecdotal evidence that HIV clinics had seen a drop in attendance. “Obviously this is not good for the HIV response because people are going without treatment, they’re not going to get tested,” she said.

“The consequences are really bad and it’s sad because Senegal was a country that was doing well with their HIV response. They are shooting themselves in the foot.”

She said while the law criminalising deliberate HIV transmission was not part of the reforms to the penal code this year, there had been an “unprecedented” rate of arrests in recent months. She labelled the charges “nonsensical” because it was reported that most people had either only discovered their status upon arrest; were arrested with condoms; or were on treatment that renders transmission of the virus impossible.

The report said police had breached confidentiality of ongoing criminal investigations involving suspected LGBTQ+ people by leaking details to the media, which reported personal and confidential information, including HIV status – exposing individuals to social stigma, family rejection, threats and violence.

LGBTQ+ people interviewed by Human Rights Watch said the crackdown was instilling fear among their community, and causing them to feel anxious and depressed. Many have gone into hiding, restricted their movements or relocated; some have left the country.

The report pointed out that the crackdown flew in the face of domestic and international laws that guaranteed the right to a fair trial, privacy and non-discrimination.

The changes to Senegal’s penal code is part of a trend across sub-Saharan Africa towards more punitive legislation directed against LGBTQ+ people.

There have been dozens of arrests in Niger since it criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February. It was the first time in the country’s history that homosexuality had been criminalised, and followed the introduction of similar laws and penal codes in neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso within the past two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.

In May, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed legislation criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which has not been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of legislation first proposed in 2021. In 2023, Uganda’s Anti-Homosexuality Act made homosexual acts punishable by death.

world.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story
world.snippet: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers The Zimbabwean ...
world.content:
The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”

Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.

Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.

She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”

Kundizeza responded in a statement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.

“I look forward to continuing to work with the Caine prize team, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”

Similar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir won the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prize with The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.

Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) was removed from the longlist of France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.

The Caine prize said in a statement that it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”

Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.

Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.

“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”

Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.

In his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”

Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journal article that found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.

world.title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
world.snippet: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr Guinea-Bissau has not approve...
world.content:
Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.

The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.

Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.

But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.

“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.

“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.

He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).

The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year.

The claims made in nearly all of their papers are “highly misleading”, said Charlotte Strøm, a Danish researcher who has co-authored research showing that Aaby, Stabell Benn, and their co-authors had no significant findings in 24 out of 25 studies and that they’ve chosen not to publish research that may not support their viewpoints.

“When researchers operate like this and abandon proper methodological rigor, they literally decide on the results themselves, and that is not science,” Strøm said, calling it “problematic, questionable [and] unethical”.

She added: “I believe there is serious cause for concern.”

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight”.

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.

In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.

“It’s completely unethical that this trial is even proposed,” because a safe and effective vaccine has been available for decades, said BK Titanji, a researcher at Emory University.

It’s “reassuring” to see Guinea-Bissau pushing back on the trial, Titanji said, adding: “A study like this one needs the highest level of ethical scrutiny. You are going to be conducting a study on the most vulnerable population, which is newborn babies, in a country that is resource-constrained.”

When Titanji recently applied for approval of a collaborative study in Cameroon, she had to include extensive documentation in her application – and it was a survey, not medical research on human subjects, she said. “I can’t come to Emory’s [institutional review board] and just be like: ‘I got permission from Cameroon.’ I have to provide the document.”

The researchers should release these documents and an updated protocol showing how the study would be conducted, she said.

Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neocolonialist” and “damaging”.

“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”

It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.

Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”

It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The ​study has ⁠not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.

At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.

The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life. Hepatitis B is widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects.

Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “canceled or suspended”.

Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira, said in February.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a February statement pushing back on the trial.

world.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
world.snippet: Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers A controversial research trial ...
world.content:
A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.

It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.

Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.

Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.

The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.

The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported by Rolling Stone. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.

According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

  • This article was amended on 13 October 2026. A previous version said CIDRAP first reported news that the research trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee. Rolling Stone had actually reported the news first.

world.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
world.snippet: Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza The Nobel peace...
world.content:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.

Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”

In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.

“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.

“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”

Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

The ICJ, a UN body, rules on disputes between states, while the international criminal court (ICC) investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of atrocities and other grave international crimes.

Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the ICC, on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.

The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.

The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.

“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.

“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.

“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.

In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.

“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.

Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.

On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”
